\\\"references/S-LINUX-IO/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"d6da925f1c90da275de1e6aa94a179a3273ad342fe77b61608a8b77fa75c3495\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"===== Documentation/block/blk-mq.rst =====\\\\n.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\\\\n\\\\n================================================\\\\nMulti-Queue Block IO Queueing Mechanism (blk-mq)\\\\n================================================\\\\n\\\\nThe Multi-Queue Block IO Queueing Mechanism is an API to enable fast storage\\\\ndevices to achieve a huge number of input/output operations per second (IOPS)\\\\nthrough queueing and submitting IO requests to block devices simultaneously,\\\\nbenefiting from the parallelism offered by modern storage devices.\\\\n\\\\nIntroduction\\\\n============\\\\n\\\\nBackground\\\\n----------\\\\n\\\\nMagnetic hard disks have been the de facto standard from the beginning of the\\\\ndevelopment of the kernel. The Block IO subsystem aimed to achieve the best\\\\nperformance possible for those devices with a high penalty when doing random\\\\naccess, and the bottleneck was the mechanical moving parts, a lot slower than\\\\nany layer on the storage stack. One example of such optimization technique\\\\ninvolves ordering read/write requests according to the current position of the\\\\nhard disk head.\\\\n\\\\nHowever, with the development of Solid State Drives and Non-Volatile Memories\\\\nwithout mechanical parts nor random access penalty and capable of performing\\\\nhigh parallel access, the bottleneck of the stack had moved from the storage\\\\ndevice to the operating system. In order to take advantage of the parallelism\\\\nin those devices' design, the multi-queue mechanism was introduced.\\\\n\\\\nThe former design had a single queue to store block IO requests with a single\\\\nlock. That did not scale well in SMP systems due to dirty data in cache and the\\\\nbottleneck of having a single lock for multiple processors. This setup also\\\\nsuffered with congestion when different processes (or the same process, moving\\\\nto different CPUs) wanted to perform block IO. Instead of this, the blk-mq API\\\\nspawns multiple queues with individual entry points local to the CPU, removing\\\\nthe need for a lock. A deeper explanation on how this works is covered in the\\\\nfollowing section (`Operation`_).\\\\n\\\\nOperation\\\\n---------\\\\n\\\\nWhen the userspace performs IO to a block device (reading or writing a file,\\\\nfor instance), blk-mq takes action: it will store and manage IO requests to\\\\nthe block device, acting as middleware between the userspace (and a file\\\\nsystem, if present) and the block device driver.\\\\n\\\\nblk-mq has two group of queues: software staging queues and hardware dispatch\\\\nqueues. When the request arrives at the block layer, it will try the shortest\\\\npath possible: send it directly to the hardware queue. However, there are two\\\\ncases that it might not do that: if there's an IO scheduler attached at the\\\\nlayer or if we want to try to merge requests. In both cases, requests will be\\\\nsent to the software queue.\\\\n\\\\nThen, after the requests are processed by software queues, they will be placed\\\\nat the hardware queue, a second stage queue where the hardware has direct access\\\\nto process those requests. However, if the hardware does not have enough\\\\nresources to accept more requests, blk-mq will place requests on a temporary\\\\nqueue, to be sent in the future, when the hardware is able.\\\\n\\\\nSoftware staging queues\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nThe block IO subsystem adds requests in the software staging queues\\\\n(represented by struct blk_mq_ctx) in case that they weren't sent\\\\ndirectly to the driver. A request is one or more BIOs. They arrived at the\\\\nblock layer through the data structure struct bio. The block layer\\\\nwill then build a new structure from it, the struct request that will\\\\nbe used to communicate with the device driver. Each queue has its own lock and\\\\nthe number of queues is defined by a per-CPU or per-node basis.\\\\n\\\\nThe staging queue can be used to merge requests for adjacent sectors. For\\\\ninstance, requests for sector 3-6, 6-7, 7-9 can become one request for 3-9.\\\\nEven if random access to SSDs and NVMs have the same time of response compared\\\\nto sequential access, grouped requests for sequential access decreases the\\\\nnumber of individual requests. This technique of merging requests is called\\\\nplugging.\\\\n\\\\nAlong with that, the requests can be reordered to ensure fairness of system\\\\nresources (e.g. to ensure that no application suffers from starvation) and/or to\\\\nimprove IO performance, by an IO scheduler.\\\\n\\\\nIO Schedulers\\\\n^^^^^^^^^^^^^\\\\n\\\\nThere are several schedulers implemented by the block layer, each one following\\\\na heuristic to improve the IO performance. They are \\\\\\\"pluggable\\\\\\\" (as in plug\\\\nand play), in the sense of they can be selected at run time using sysfs. You\\\\ncan read more about Linux's IO schedulers `here\\\\n<https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/block/index.html>`_. The scheduling\\\\nhappens only between requests in the same queue, so it is not possible to merge\\\\nrequests from different queues, otherwise there would be cache trashing and a\\\\nneed to have a lock for each queue. After the scheduling, the requests are\\\\neligible to be sent to the hardware. One of the possible schedulers to be\\\\nselected is the NONE scheduler, the most straightforward one. It will just\\\\nplace requests on whatever software queue the process is running on, without\\\\nany reordering. When the device starts processing requests in the hardware\\\\nqueue (a.k.a. run the hardware queue), the software queues mapped to that\\\\nhardware queue will be drained in sequence according to their mapping.\\\\n\\\\nHardware dispatch queues\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nThe hardware queue (represented by struct blk_mq_hw_ctx) is a struct\\\\nused by device drivers to map the device submission queues (or device DMA ring\\\\nbuffer), and are the last step of the block layer submission code before the\\\\nlow level device driver taking ownership of the request. To run this queue, the\\\\nblock layer removes requests from the associated software queues and tries to\\\\ndispatch to the hardware.\\\\n\\\\nIf it's not possible to send the requests directly to hardware, they will be\\\\nadded to a linked list (``hctx->dispatch``) of requests. Then,\\\\nnext time the block layer runs a queue, it will send the requests laying at the\\\\n``dispatch`` list first, to ensure a fairness dispatch with those\\\\nrequests that were ready to be sent first. The number of hardware queues\\\\ndepends on the number of hardware contexts supported by the hardware and its\\\\ndevice driver, but it will not be more than the number of cores of the system.\\\\nThere is no reordering at this stage, and each software queue has a set of\\\\nhardware queues to send requests for.\\\\n\\\\n.. note::\\\\n\\\\n        Neither the block layer nor the device protocols guarantee\\\\n        the order of completion of requests. This must be handled by\\\\n        higher layers, like the filesystem.\\\\n\\\\nTag-based completion\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nIn order to indicate which request has been completed, every request is\\\\nidentified by an integer, ranging from 0 to the dispatch queue size. This tag\\\\nis generated by the block layer and later reused by the device driver, removing\\\\nthe need to create a redundant identifier. When a request is completed in the\\\\ndriver, the tag is sent back to the block layer to notify it of the finalization.\\\\nThis removes the need to do a linear search to find out which IO has been\\\\ncompleted.\\\\n\\\\nFurther reading\\\\n---------------\\\\n\\\\n- `Linux Block IO: Introducing Multi-queue SSD Access on Multi-core Systems <http://kernel.dk/blk-mq.pdf>`_\\\\n\\\\n- `NOOP scheduler <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noop_scheduler>`_\\\\n\\\\n- `Null block device driver <https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/block/null_blk.html>`_\\\\n\\\\nSource code documentation\\\\n=========================\\\\n\\\\n.. kernel-doc:: include/linux/blk-mq.h\\\\n\\\\n.. kernel-doc:: block/blk-mq.c\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n===== Documentation/filesystems/iomap/design.rst =====\\\\n.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\\\\n.. _iomap_design:\\\\n\\\\n..\\\\n        Dumb style notes to maintain the author's sanity:\\\\n        Please try to start sentences on separate lines so that\\\\n        sentence changes don't bleed colors in diff.\\\\n        Heading decorations are documented in sphinx.rst.\\\\n\\\\n==============\\\\nLibrary Design\\\\n==============\\\\n\\\\n.. contents:: Table of Contents\\\\n   :local:\\\\n\\\\nIntroduction\\\\n============\\\\n\\\\niomap is a filesystem library for handling common file operations.\\\\nThe library has two layers:\\\\n\\\\n 1. A lower layer that provides an iterator over ranges of file offsets.\\\\n    This layer tries to obtain mappings of each file ranges to storage\\\\n    from the filesystem, but the storage information is not necessarily\\\\n    required.\\\\n\\\\n 2. An upper layer that acts upon the space mappings provided by the\\\\n    lower layer iterator.\\\\n\\\\nThe iteration can involve mappings of file's logical offset ranges to\\\\nphysical extents, but the storage layer information is not necessarily\\\\nrequired, e.g. for walking cached file information.\\\\nThe library exports various APIs for implementing file operations such\\\\nas:\\\\n\\\\n * Pagecache reads and writes\\\\n * Folio write faults to the pagecache\\\\n * Writeback of dirty folios\\\\n * Direct I/O reads and writes\\\\n * fsdax I/O reads, writes, loads, and stores\\\\n * FIEMAP\\\\n * lseek ``SEEK_DATA`` and ``SEEK_HOLE``\\\\n * swapfile activation\\\\n\\\\nThis origins of this library is the file I/O path that XFS once used; it\\\\nhas now been extended to cover several other operations.\\\\n\\\\nWho Should Read This?\\\\n=====================\\\\n\\\\nThe target audience for this document are filesystem, storage, and\\\\npagecache programmers and code reviewers.\\\\n\\\\nIf you are working on PCI, machine architectures, or device drivers, you\\\\nare most likely in the wrong place.\\\\n\\\\nHow Is This Better?\\\\n===================\\\\n\\\\nUnlike the classic Linux I/O model which breaks file I/O into small\\\\nunits (generally memory pages or blocks) and looks up space mappings on\\\\nthe basis of that unit, the iomap model asks the filesystem for the\\\\nlargest space mappings that it can create for a given file operation and\\\\ninitiates operations on that basis.\\\\nThis strategy improves the filesystem's visibility into the size of the\\\\noperation being performed, which enables it to combat fragmentation with\\\\nlarger space allocations when possible.\\\\nLarger space mappings improve runtime performance by amortizing the cost\\\\nof mapping function calls into the filesystem across a larger amount of\\\\ndata.\\\\n\\\\nAt a high level, an iomap operation `looks like this\\\\n<https://lore.kernel.org/all/ZGbVaewzcCysclPt@dread.disaster.area/>`_:\\\\n\\\\n1. For each byte in the operation range...\\\\n\\\\n   1. Obtain a space mapping via ``->iomap_begin``\\\\n\\\\n   2. For each sub-unit of work...\\\\n\\\\n      1. Revalidate the mapping and go back to (1) above, if necessary.\\\\n         So far only the pagecache operations need to do this.\\\\n\\\\n      2. Do the work\\\\n\\\\n   3. Increment operation cursor\\\\n\\\\n   4. Release the mapping via ``->iomap_end``, if necessary\\\\n\\\\nEach iomap operation will be covered in more detail below.\\\\nThis library was covered previously by an `LWN article\\\\n<https://lwn.net/Articles/935934/>`_ and a `KernelNewbies page\\\\n<https://kernelnewbies.org/KernelProjects/iomap>`_.\\\\n\\\\nThe goal of this document is to provide a brief discussion of the\\\\ndesign and capabilities of iomap, followed by a more detailed catalog\\\\nof the interfaces presented by iomap.\\\\nIf you change iomap, please update this design document.\\\\n\\\\nFile Range Iterator\\\\n===================\\\\n\\\\nDefinitions\\\\n-----------\\\\n\\\\n * **buffer head**: Shattered remnants of the old buffer cache.\\\\n\\\\n * ``fsblock``: The block size of a file, also known as ``i_blocksize``.\\\\n\\\\n * ``i_rwsem``: The VFS ``struct inode`` rwsemaphore.\\\\n   Processes hold this in shared mode to read file state and contents.\\\\n   Some filesystems may allow shared mode for writes.\\\\n   Processes often hold this in exclusive mode to change file state and\\\\n   contents.\\\\n\\\\n * ``invalidate_lock``: The pagecache ``struct address_space``\\\\n   rwsemaphore that protects against folio insertion and removal for\\\\n   filesystems that support punching out folios below EOF.\\\\n   Processes wishing to insert folios must hold this lock in shared\\\\n   mode to prevent removal, though concurrent insertion is allowed.\\\\n   Processes wishing to remove folios must hold this lock in exclusive\\\\n   mode to prevent insertions.\\\\n   Concurrent removals are not allowed.\\\\n\\\\n * ``dax_read_lock``: The RCU read lock that dax takes to prevent a\\\\n   device pre-shutdown hook from returning before other threads have\\\\n   released resources.\\\\n\\\\n * **filesystem mapping lock**: This synchronization primitive is\\\\n   internal to the filesystem and must protect the file mapping data\\\\n   from updates while a mapping is being sampled.\\\\n   The filesystem author must determine how this coordination should\\\\n   happen; it does not need to be an actual lock.\\\\n\\\\n * **iomap internal operation lock**: This is a general term for\\\\n   synchronization primitives that iomap functions take while holding a\\\\n   mapping.\\\\n   A specific example would be taking the folio lock while reading or\\\\n   writing the pagecache.\\\\n\\\\n * **pure overwrite**: A write operation that does not require any\\\\n   metadata or zeroing operations to perform during either submission\\\\n   or completion.\\\\n   This implies that the filesystem must have already allocated space\\\\n   on disk as ``IOMAP_MAPPED`` and the filesystem must not place any\\\\n   constraints on IO alignment or size.\\\\n   The only constraints on I/O alignment are device level (minimum I/O\\\\n   size and alignment, typically sector size).\\\\n\\\\n``struct iomap``\\\\n----------------\\\\n\\\\nThe filesystem communicates to the iomap iterator the mapping of\\\\nbyte ranges of a file to byte ranges of a storage device with the\\\\nstructure below:\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: c\\\\n\\\\n struct iomap {\\\\n     u64                 addr;\\\\n     loff_t              offset;\\\\n     u64                 length;\\\\n     u16                 type;\\\\n     u16                 flags;\\\\n     struct block_device *bdev;\\\\n     struct dax_device   *dax_dev;\\\\n     void                *inline_data;\\\\n     void                *private;\\\\n     const struct iomap_folio_ops *folio_ops;\\\\n     u64                 validity_cookie;\\\\n };\\\\n\\\\nThe fields are as follows:\\\\n\\\\n * ``offset`` and ``length`` describe the range of file offsets, in\\\\n   bytes, covered by this mapping.\\\\n   These fields must always be set by the filesystem.\\\\n\\\\n * ``type`` describes the type of the space mapping:\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_HOLE**: No storage has been allocated.\\\\n     This type must never be returned in response to an ``IOMAP_WRITE``\\\\n     operation because writes must allocate and map space, and return\\\\n     the mapping.\\\\n     The ``addr`` field must be set to ``IOMAP_NULL_ADDR``.\\\\n     iomap does not support writing (whether via pagecache or direct\\\\n     I/O) to a hole.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_DELALLOC**: A promise to allocate space at a later time\\\\n     (\\\\\\\"delayed allocation\\\\\\\").\\\\n     If the filesystem returns IOMAP_F_NEW here and the write fails, the\\\\n     ``->iomap_end`` function must delete the reservation.\\\\n     The ``addr`` field must be set to ``IOMAP_NULL_ADDR``.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_MAPPED**: The file range maps to specific space on the\\\\n     storage device.\\\\n     The device is returned in ``bdev`` or ``dax_dev``.\\\\n     The device address, in bytes, is returned via ``addr``.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_UNWRITTEN**: The file range maps to specific space on the\\\\n     storage device, but the space has not yet been initialized.\\\\n     The device is returned in ``bdev`` or ``dax_dev``.\\\\n     The device address, in bytes, is returned via ``addr``.\\\\n     Reads from this type of mapping will return zeroes to the caller.\\\\n     For a write or writeback operation, the ioend should update the\\\\n     mapping to MAPPED.\\\\n     Refer to the sections about ioends for more details.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_INLINE**: The file range maps to the memory buffer\\\\n     specified by ``inline_data``.\\\\n     For write operation, the ``->iomap_end`` function presumably\\\\n     handles persisting the data.\\\\n     The ``addr`` field must be set to ``IOMAP_NULL_ADDR``.\\\\n\\\\n * ``flags`` describe the status of the space mapping.\\\\n   These flags should be set by the filesystem in ``->iomap_begin``:\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_NEW**: The space under the mapping is newly allocated.\\\\n     Areas that will not be written to must be zeroed.\\\\n     If a write fails and the mapping is a space reservation, the\\\\n     reservation must be deleted.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_DIRTY**: The inode will have uncommitted metadata needed\\\\n     to access any data written.\\\\n     fdatasync is required to commit these changes to persistent\\\\n     storage.\\\\n     This needs to take into account metadata changes that *may* be made\\\\n     at I/O completion, such as file size updates from direct I/O.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_SHARED**: The space under the mapping is shared.\\\\n     Copy on write is necessary to avoid corrupting other file data.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_BUFFER_HEAD**: This mapping requires the use of buffer\\\\n     heads for pagecache operations.\\\\n     Do not add more uses of this.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_MERGED**: Multiple contiguous block mappings were\\\\n     coalesced into this single mapping.\\\\n     This is only useful for FIEMAP.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_XATTR**: The mapping is for extended attribute data, not\\\\n     regular file data.\\\\n     This is only useful for FIEMAP.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_PRIVATE**: Starting with this value, the upper bits can\\\\n     be set by the filesystem for its own purposes.\\\\n\\\\n   These flags can be set by iomap itself during file operations.\\\\n   The filesystem should supply an ``->iomap_end`` function if it needs\\\\n   to observe these flags:\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_SIZE_CHANGED**: The file size has changed as a result of\\\\n     using this mapping.\\\\n\\\\n   * **IOMAP_F_STALE**: The mapping was found to be stale.\\\\n     iomap will call ``->iomap_end`` on this mapping and then\\\\n     ``->iomap_begin`` to obtain a new mapping.\\\\n\\\\n   Currently, these flags are only set by pagecache operations.\\\\n\\\\n * ``addr`` describes the device address, in bytes.\\\\n\\\\n * ``bdev`` describes the block device for this mapping.\\\\n   This only needs to be set for mapped or unwritten operations.\\\\n\\\\n * ``dax_dev`` describes the DAX device for this mapping.\\\\n   This only needs to be set for mapped or unwritten operations, and\\\\n   only for a fsdax operation.\\\\n\\\\n * ``inline_data`` points to a memory buffer for I/O involving\\\\n   ``IOMAP_INLINE`` mappings.\\\\n   This value is ignored for all other mapping types.\\\\n\\\\n * ``private`` is a pointer to `filesystem-private information\\\\n   <https://lore.kernel.org/all/20180619164137.13720-7-hch@lst.de/>`_.\\\\n   This value will be passed unchanged to ``->iomap_end``.\\\\n\\\\n * ``folio_ops`` will be covered in the section on pagecache operations.\\\\n\\\\n * ``validity_cookie`` is a magic freshness value set by the filesystem\\\\n   that should be used to detect stale mappings.\\\\n   For pagecache operations this is critical for correct operation\\\\n   because page faults can occur, which implies that filesystem locks\\\\n   should not be held between ``->iomap_begin`` and ``->iomap_end``.\\\\n   Filesystems with completely static mappings need not set this value.\\\\n   Only pagecache operations revalidate mappings; see the section about\\\\n   ``iomap_valid`` for details.\\\\n\\\\n``struct iomap_ops``\\\\n--------------------\\\\n\\\\nEvery iomap function requires the filesystem to pass an operations\\\\nstructure to obtain a mapping and (optionally) to release the mapping:\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: c\\\\n\\\\n struct iomap_ops {\\\\n     int (*iomap_begin)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos, loff_t length,\\\\n                        unsigned flags, struct iomap *iomap,\\\\n                        struct iomap *srcmap);\\\\n\\\\n     int (*iomap_end)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos, loff_t length,\\\\n                      ssize_t written, unsigned flags,\\\\n                      struct iomap *iomap);\\\\n };\\\\n\\\\n``->iomap_begin``\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\niomap operations call ``->iomap_begin`` to obtain one file mapping for\\\\nthe range of bytes specified by ``pos`` and ``length`` for the file\\\\n``inode``.\\\\nThis mapping should be returned through the ``iomap`` pointer.\\\\nThe mapping must cover at least the first byte of the supplied file\\\\nrange, but it does not need to cover the entire requested range.\\\\n\\\\nEach iomap operation describes the requested operation through the\\\\n``flags`` argument.\\\\nThe exact value of ``flags`` will be documented in the\\\\noperation-specific sections below.\\\\nThese flags can, at least in principle, apply generally to iomap\\\\noperations:\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_DIRECT`` is set when the caller wishes to issue file I/O to\\\\n   block storage.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_DAX`` is set when the caller wishes to issue file I/O to\\\\n   memory-like storage.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_NOWAIT`` is set when the caller wishes to perform a best\\\\n   effort attempt to avoid any operation that would result in blocking\\\\n   the submitting task.\\\\n   This is similar in intent to ``O_NONBLOCK`` for network APIs - it is\\\\n   intended for asynchronous applications to keep doing other work\\\\n   instead of waiting for the specific unavailable filesystem resource\\\\n   to become available.\\\\n   Filesystems implementing ``IOMAP_NOWAIT`` semantics need to use\\\\n   trylock algorithms.\\\\n   They need to be able to satisfy the entire I/O request range with a\\\\n   single iomap mapping.\\\\n   They need to avoid reading or writing metadata synchronously.\\\\n   They need to avoid blocking memory allocations.\\\\n   They need to avoid waiting on transaction reservations to allow\\\\n   modifications to take place.\\\\n   They probably should not be allocating new space.\\\\n   And so on.\\\\n   If there is any doubt in the filesystem developer's mind as to\\\\n   whether any specific ``IOMAP_NOWAIT`` operation may end up blocking,\\\\n   then they should return ``-EAGAIN`` as early as possible rather than\\\\n   start the operation and force the submitting task to block.\\\\n   ``IOMAP_NOWAIT`` is often set on behalf of ``IOCB_NOWAIT`` or\\\\n   ``RWF_NOWAIT``.\\\\n\\\\nIf it is necessary to read existing file contents from a `different\\\\n<https://lore.kernel.org/all/20191008071527.29304-9-hch@lst.de/>`_\\\\ndevice or address range on a device, the filesystem should return that\\\\ninformation via ``srcmap``.\\\\nOnly pagecache and fsdax operations support reading from one mapping and\\\\nwriting to another.\\\\n\\\\n``->iomap_end``\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nAfter the operation completes, the ``->iomap_end`` function, if present,\\\\nis called to signal that iomap is finished with a mapping.\\\\nTypically, implementations will use this function to tear down any\\\\ncontext that were set up in ``->iomap_begin``.\\\\nFor example, a write might wish to commit the reservations for the bytes\\\\nthat were operated upon and unreserve any space that was not operated\\\\nupon.\\\\n``written`` might be zero if no bytes were touched.\\\\n``flags`` will contain the same value passed to ``->iomap_begin``.\\\\niomap ops for reads are not likely to need to supply this function.\\\\n\\\\nBoth functions should return a negative errno code on error, or zero on\\\\nsuccess.\\\\n\\\\nPreparing for File Operations\\\\n=============================\\\\n\\\\niomap only handles mapping and I/O.\\\\nFilesystems must still call out to the VFS to check input parameters\\\\nand file state before initiating an I/O operation.\\\\nIt does not handle obtaining filesystem freeze protection, updating of\\\\ntimestamps, stripping privileges, or access control.\\\\n\\\\nLocking Hierarchy\\\\n=================\\\\n\\\\niomap requires that filesystems supply their own locking model.\\\\nThere are three categories of synchronization primitives, as far as\\\\niomap is concerned:\\\\n\\\\n * The **upper** level primitive is provided by the filesystem to\\\\n   coordinate access to different iomap operations.\\\\n   The exact primitive is specific to the filesystem and operation,\\\\n   but is often a VFS inode, pagecache invalidation, or folio lock.\\\\n   For example, a filesystem might take ``i_rwsem`` before calling\\\\n   ``iomap_file_buffered_write`` and ``iomap_file_unshare`` to prevent\\\\n   these two file operations from clobbering each other.\\\\n   Pagecache writeback may lock a folio to prevent other threads from\\\\n   accessing the folio until writeback is underway.\\\\n\\\\n   * The **lower** level primitive is taken by the filesystem in the\\\\n     ``->iomap_begin`` and ``->iomap_end`` functions to coordinate\\\\n     access to the file space mapping information.\\\\n     The fields of the iomap object should be filled out while holding\\\\n     this primitive.\\\\n     The upper level synchronization primitive, if any, remains held\\\\n     while acquiring the lower level synchronization primitive.\\\\n     For example, XFS takes ``ILOCK_EXCL`` and ext4 takes ``i_data_sem``\\\\n     while sampling mappings.\\\\n     Filesystems with immutable mapping information may not require\\\\n     synchronization here.\\\\n\\\\n   * The **operation** primitive is taken by an iomap operation to\\\\n     coordinate access to its own internal data structures.\\\\n     The upper level synchronization primitive, if any, remains held\\\\n     while acquiring this primitive.\\\\n     The lower level primitive is not held while acquiring this\\\\n     primitive.\\\\n     For example, pagecache write operations will obtain a file mapping,\\\\n     then grab and lock a folio to copy new contents.\\\\n     It may also lock an internal folio state object to update metadata.\\\\n\\\\nThe exact locking requirements are specific to the filesystem; for\\\\ncertain operations, some of these locks can be elided.\\\\nAll further mentions of locking are *recommendations*, not mandates.\\\\nEach filesystem author must figure out the locking for themself.\\\\n\\\\nBugs and Limitations\\\\n====================\\\\n\\\\n * No support for fscrypt.\\\\n * No support for compression.\\\\n * No support for fsverity yet.\\\\n * Strong assumptions that IO should work the way it does on XFS.\\\\n * Does iomap *actually* work for non-regular file data?\\\\n\\\\nPatches welcome!\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n===== Documentation/filesystems/iomap/operations.rst =====\\\\n.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\\\\n.. _iomap_operations:\\\\n\\\\n..\\\\n        Dumb style notes to maintain the author's sanity:\\\\n        Please try to start sentences on separate lines so that\\\\n        sentence changes don't bleed colors in diff.\\\\n        Heading decorations are documented in sphinx.rst.\\\\n\\\\n=========================\\\\nSupported File Operations\\\\n=========================\\\\n\\\\n.. contents:: Table of Contents\\\\n   :local:\\\\n\\\\nBelow are a discussion of the high level file operations that iomap\\\\nimplements.\\\\n\\\\nBuffered I/O\\\\n============\\\\n\\\\nBuffered I/O is the default file I/O path in Linux.\\\\nFile contents are cached in memory (\\\\\\\"pagecache\\\\\\\") to satisfy reads and\\\\nwrites.\\\\nDirty cache will be written back to disk at some point that can be\\\\nforced via ``fsync`` and variants.\\\\n\\\\niomap implements nearly all the folio and pagecache management that\\\\nfilesystems have to implement themselves under the legacy I/O model.\\\\nThis means that the filesystem need not know the details of allocating,\\\\nmapping, managing uptodate and dirty state, or writeback of pagecache\\\\nfolios.\\\\nUnder the legacy I/O model, this was managed very inefficiently with\\\\nlinked lists of buffer heads instead of the per-folio bitmaps that iomap\\\\nuses.\\\\nUnless the filesystem explicitly opts in to buffer heads, they will not\\\\nbe used, which makes buffered I/O much more efficient, and the pagecache\\\\nmaintainer much happier.\\\\n\\\\n``struct address_space_operations``\\\\n-----------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nThe following iomap functions can be referenced directly from the\\\\naddress space operations structure:\\\\n\\\\n * ``iomap_dirty_folio``\\\\n * ``iomap_release_folio``\\\\n * ``iomap_invalidate_folio``\\\\n * ``iomap_is_partially_uptodate``\\\\n\\\\nThe following address space operations can be wrapped easily:\\\\n\\\\n * ``read_folio``\\\\n * ``readahead``\\\\n * ``writepages``\\\\n * ``bmap``\\\\n * ``swap_activate``\\\\n\\\\n``struct iomap_folio_ops``\\\\n--------------------------\\\\n\\\\nThe ``->iomap_begin`` function for pagecache operations may set the\\\\n``struct iomap::folio_ops`` field to an ops structure to override\\\\ndefault behaviors of iomap:\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: c\\\\n\\\\n struct iomap_folio_ops {\\\\n     struct folio *(*get_folio)(struct iomap_iter *iter, loff_t pos,\\\\n                                unsigned len);\\\\n     void (*put_folio)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos, unsigned copied,\\\\n                       struct folio *folio);\\\\n     bool (*iomap_valid)(struct inode *inode, const struct iomap *iomap);\\\\n };\\\\n\\\\niomap calls these functions:\\\\n\\\\n  - ``get_folio``: Called to allocate and return an active reference to\\\\n    a locked folio prior to starting a write.\\\\n    If this function is not provided, iomap will call\\\\n    ``iomap_get_folio``.\\\\n    This could be used to `set up per-folio filesystem state\\\\n    <https://lore.kernel.org/all/20190429220934.10415-5-agruenba@redhat.com/>`_\\\\n    for a write.\\\\n\\\\n  - ``put_folio``: Called to unlock and put a folio after a pagecache\\\\n    operation completes.\\\\n    If this function is not provided, iomap will ``folio_unlock`` and\\\\n    ``folio_put`` on its own.\\\\n    This could be used to `commit per-folio filesystem state\\\\n    <https://lore.kernel.org/all/20180619164137.13720-6-hch@lst.de/>`_\\\\n    that was set up by ``->get_folio``.\\\\n\\\\n  - ``iomap_valid``: The filesystem may not hold locks between\\\\n    ``->iomap_begin`` and ``->iomap_end`` because pagecache operations\\\\n    can take folio locks, fault on userspace pages, initiate writeback\\\\n    for memory reclamation, or engage in other time-consuming actions.\\\\n    If a file's space mapping data are mutable, it is possible that the\\\\n    mapping for a particular pagecache folio can `change in the time it\\\\n    takes\\\\n    <https://lore.kernel.org/all/20221123055812.747923-8-david@fromorbit.com/>`_\\\\n    to allocate, install, and lock that folio.\\\\n\\\\n    For the pagecache, races can happen if writeback doesn't take\\\\n    ``i_rwsem`` or ``invalidate_lock`` and updates mapping information.\\\\n    Races can also happen if the filesytem allows concurrent writes.\\\\n    For such files, the mapping *must* be revalidated after the folio\\\\n    lock has been taken so that iomap can manage the folio correctly.\\\\n\\\\n    fsdax does not need this revalidation because there's no writeback\\\\n    and no support for unwritten extents.\\\\n\\\\n    Filesystems subject to this kind of race must provide a\\\\n    ``->iomap_valid`` function to decide if the mapping is still valid.\\\\n    If the mapping is not valid, the mapping will be sampled again.\\\\n\\\\n    To support making the validity decision, the filesystem's\\\\n    ``->iomap_begin`` function may set ``struct iomap::validity_cookie``\\\\n    at the same time that it populates the other iomap fields.\\\\n    A simple validation cookie implementation is a sequence counter.\\\\n    If the filesystem bumps the sequence counter every time it modifies\\\\n    the inode's extent map, it can be placed in the ``struct\\\\n    iomap::validity_cookie`` during ``->iomap_begin``.\\\\n    If the value in the cookie is found to be different to the value\\\\n    the filesystem holds when the mapping is passed back to\\\\n    ``->iomap_valid``, then the iomap should considered stale and the\\\\n    validation failed.\\\\n\\\\nThese ``struct kiocb`` flags are significant for buffered I/O with iomap:\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOCB_NOWAIT``: Turns on ``IOMAP_NOWAIT``.\\\\n\\\\nInternal per-Folio State\\\\n------------------------\\\\n\\\\nIf the fsblock size matches the size of a pagecache folio, it is assumed\\\\nthat all disk I/O operations will operate on the entire folio.\\\\nThe uptodate (memory contents are at least as new as what's on disk) and\\\\ndirty (memory contents are newer than what's on disk) status of the\\\\nfolio are all that's needed for this case.\\\\n\\\\nIf the fsblock size is less than the size of a pagecache folio, iomap\\\\ntracks the per-fsblock uptodate and dirty state itself.\\\\nThis enables iomap to handle both \\\\\\\"bs < ps\\\\\\\" `filesystems\\\\n<https://lore.kernel.org/all/20230725122932.144426-1-ritesh.list@gmail.com/>`_\\\\nand large folios in the pagecache.\\\\n\\\\niomap internally tracks two state bits per fsblock:\\\\n\\\\n * ``uptodate``: iomap will try to keep folios fully up to date.\\\\n   If there are read(ahead) errors, those fsblocks will not be marked\\\\n   uptodate.\\\\n   The folio itself will be marked uptodate when all fsblocks within the\\\\n   folio are uptodate.\\\\n\\\\n * ``dirty``: iomap will set the per-block dirty state when programs\\\\n   write to the file.\\\\n   The folio itself will be marked dirty when any fsblock within the\\\\n   folio is dirty.\\\\n\\\\niomap also tracks the amount of read and write disk IOs that are in\\\\nflight.\\\\nThis structure is much lighter weight than ``struct buffer_head``\\\\nbecause there is only one per folio, and the per-fsblock overhead is two\\\\nbits vs. 104 bytes.\\\\n\\\\nFilesystems wishing to turn on large folios in the pagecache should call\\\\n``mapping_set_large_folios`` when initializing the incore inode.\\\\n\\\\nBuffered Readahead and Reads\\\\n----------------------------\\\\n\\\\nThe ``iomap_readahead`` function initiates readahead to the pagecache.\\\\nThe ``iomap_read_folio`` function reads one folio's worth of data into\\\\nthe pagecache.\\\\nThe ``flags`` argument to ``->iomap_begin`` will be set to zero.\\\\nThe pagecache takes whatever locks it needs before calling the\\\\nfilesystem.\\\\n\\\\nBuffered Writes\\\\n---------------\\\\n\\\\nThe ``iomap_file_buffered_write`` function writes an ``iocb`` to the\\\\npagecache.\\\\n``IOMAP_WRITE`` or ``IOMAP_WRITE`` | ``IOMAP_NOWAIT`` will be passed as\\\\nthe ``flags`` argument to ``->iomap_begin``.\\\\nCallers commonly take ``i_rwsem`` in either shared or exclusive mode\\\\nbefore calling this function.\\\\n\\\\nmmap Write Faults\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nThe ``iomap_page_mkwrite`` function handles a write fault to a folio in\\\\nthe pagecache.\\\\n``IOMAP_WRITE | IOMAP_FAULT`` will be passed as the ``flags`` argument\\\\nto ``->iomap_begin``.\\\\nCallers commonly take the mmap ``invalidate_lock`` in shared or\\\\nexclusive mode before calling this function.\\\\n\\\\nBuffered Write Failures\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nAfter a short write to the pagecache, the areas not written will not\\\\nbecome marked dirty.\\\\nThe filesystem must arrange to `cancel\\\\n<https://lore.kernel.org/all/20221123055812.747923-6-david@fromorbit.com/>`_\\\\nsuch `reservations\\\\n<https://lore.kernel.org/linux-xfs/20220817093627.GZ3600936@dread.disaster.area/>`_\\\\nbecause writeback will not consume the reservation.\\\\nThe ``iomap_write_delalloc_release`` can be called from a\\\\n``->iomap_end`` function to find all the clean areas of the folios\\\\ncaching a fresh (``IOMAP_F_NEW``) delalloc mapping.\\\\nIt takes the ``invalidate_lock``.\\\\n\\\\nThe filesystem must supply a function ``punch`` to be called for\\\\neach file range in this state.\\\\nThis function must *only* remove delayed allocation reservations, in\\\\ncase another thread racing with the current thread writes successfully\\\\nto the same region and triggers writeback to flush the dirty data out to\\\\ndisk.\\\\n\\\\nZeroing for File Operations\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nFilesystems can call ``iomap_zero_range`` to perform zeroing of the\\\\npagecache for non-truncation file operations that are not aligned to\\\\nthe fsblock size.\\\\n``IOMAP_ZERO`` will be passed as the ``flags`` argument to\\\\n``->iomap_begin``.\\\\nCallers typically hold ``i_rwsem`` and ``invalidate_lock`` in exclusive\\\\nmode before calling this function.\\\\n\\\\nUnsharing Reflinked File Data\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nFilesystems can call ``iomap_file_unshare`` to force a file sharing\\\\nstorage with another file to preemptively copy the shared data to newly\\\\nallocate storage.\\\\n``IOMAP_WRITE | IOMAP_UNSHARE`` will be passed as the ``flags`` argument\\\\nto ``->iomap_begin``.\\\\nCallers typically hold ``i_rwsem`` and ``invalidate_lock`` in exclusive\\\\nmode before calling this function.\\\\n\\\\nTruncation\\\\n----------\\\\n\\\\nFilesystems can call ``iomap_truncate_page`` to zero the bytes in the\\\\npagecache from EOF to the end of the fsblock during a file truncation\\\\noperation.\\\\n``truncate_setsize`` or ``truncate_pagecache`` will take care of\\\\neverything after the EOF block.\\\\n``IOMAP_ZERO`` will be passed as the ``flags`` argument to\\\\n``->iomap_begin``.\\\\nCallers typically hold ``i_rwsem`` and ``invalidate_lock`` in exclusive\\\\nmode before calling this function.\\\\n\\\\nPagecache Writeback\\\\n-------------------\\\\n\\\\nFilesystems can call ``iomap_writepages`` to respond to a request to\\\\nwrite dirty pagecache folios to disk.\\\\nThe ``mapping`` and ``wbc`` parameters should be passed unchanged.\\\\nThe ``wpc`` pointer should be allocated by the filesystem and must\\\\nbe initialized to zero.\\\\n\\\\nThe pagecache will lock each folio before trying to schedule it for\\\\nwriteback.\\\\nIt does not lock ``i_rwsem`` or ``invalidate_lock``.\\\\n\\\\nThe dirty bit will be cleared for all folios run through the\\\\n``->map_blocks`` machinery described below even if the writeback fails.\\\\nThis is to prevent dirty folio clots when storage devices fail; an\\\\n``-EIO`` is recorded for userspace to collect via ``fsync``.\\\\n\\\\nThe ``ops`` structure must be specified and is as follows:\\\\n\\\\n``struct iomap_writeback_ops``\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: c\\\\n\\\\n struct iomap_writeback_ops {\\\\n     int (*map_blocks)(struct iomap_writepage_ctx *wpc, struct inode *inode,\\\\n                       loff_t offset, unsigned len);\\\\n     int (*prepare_ioend)(struct iomap_ioend *ioend, int status);\\\\n     void (*discard_folio)(struct folio *folio, loff_t pos);\\\\n };\\\\n\\\\nThe fields are as follows:\\\\n\\\\n  - ``map_blocks``: Sets ``wpc->iomap`` to the space mapping of the file\\\\n    range (in bytes) given by ``offset`` and ``len``.\\\\n    iomap calls this function for each dirty fs block in each dirty folio,\\\\n    though it will `reuse mappings\\\\n    <https://lore.kernel.org/all/20231207072710.176093-15-hch@lst.de/>`_\\\\n    for runs of contiguous dirty fsblocks within a folio.\\\\n    Do not return ``IOMAP_INLINE`` mappings here; the ``->iomap_end``\\\\n    function must deal with persisting written data.\\\\n    Do not return ``IOMAP_DELALLOC`` mappings here; iomap currently\\\\n    requires mapping to allocated space.\\\\n    Filesystems can skip a potentially expensive mapping lookup if the\\\\n    mappings have not changed.\\\\n    This revalidation must be open-coded by the filesystem; it is\\\\n    unclear if ``iomap::validity_cookie`` can be reused for this\\\\n    purpose.\\\\n    This function must be supplied by the filesystem.\\\\n\\\\n  - ``prepare_ioend``: Enables filesystems to transform the writeback\\\\n    ioend or perform any other preparatory work before the writeback I/O\\\\n    is submitted.\\\\n    This might include pre-write space accounting updates, or installing\\\\n    a custom ``->bi_end_io`` function for internal purposes, such as\\\\n    deferring the ioend completion to a workqueue to run metadata update\\\\n    transactions from process context.\\\\n    This function is optional.\\\\n\\\\n  - ``discard_folio``: iomap calls this function after ``->map_blocks``\\\\n    fails to schedule I/O for any part of a dirty folio.\\\\n    The function should throw away any reservations that may have been\\\\n    made for the write.\\\\n    The folio will be marked clean and an ``-EIO`` recorded in the\\\\n    pagecache.\\\\n    Filesystems can use this callback to `remove\\\\n    <https://lore.kernel.org/all/20201029163313.1766967-1-bfoster@redhat.com/>`_\\\\n    delalloc reservations to avoid having delalloc reservations for\\\\n    clean pagecache.\\\\n    This function is optional.\\\\n\\\\nPagecache Writeback Completion\\\\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\\\n\\\\nTo handle the bookkeeping that must happen after disk I/O for writeback\\\\ncompletes, iomap creates chains of ``struct iomap_ioend`` objects that\\\\nwrap the ``bio`` that is used to write pagecache data to disk.\\\\nBy default, iomap finishes writeback ioends by clearing the writeback\\\\nbit on the folios attached to the ``ioend``.\\\\nIf the write failed, it will also set the error bits on the folios and\\\\nthe address space.\\\\nThis can happen in interrupt or process context, depending on the\\\\nstorage device.\\\\n\\\\nFilesystems that need to update internal bookkeeping (e.g. unwritten\\\\nextent conversions) should provide a ``->prepare_ioend`` function to\\\\nset ``struct iomap_end::bio::bi_end_io`` to its own function.\\\\nThis function should call ``iomap_finish_ioends`` after finishing its\\\\nown work (e.g. unwritten extent conversion).\\\\n\\\\nSome filesystems may wish to `amortize the cost of running metadata\\\\ntransactions\\\\n<https://lore.kernel.org/all/20220120034733.221737-1-david@fromorbit.com/>`_\\\\nfor post-writeback updates by batching them.\\\\nThey may also require transactions to run from process context, which\\\\nimplies punting batches to a workqueue.\\\\niomap ioends contain a ``list_head`` to enable batching.\\\\n\\\\nGiven a batch of ioends, iomap has a few helpers to assist with\\\\namortization:\\\\n\\\\n * ``iomap_sort_ioends``: Sort all the ioends in the list by file\\\\n   offset.\\\\n\\\\n * ``iomap_ioend_try_merge``: Given an ioend that is not in any list and\\\\n   a separate list of sorted ioends, merge as many of the ioends from\\\\n   the head of the list into the given ioend.\\\\n   ioends can only be merged if the file range and storage addresses are\\\\n   contiguous; the unwritten and shared status are the same; and the\\\\n   write I/O outcome is the same.\\\\n   The merged ioends become their own list.\\\\n\\\\n * ``iomap_finish_ioends``: Finish an ioend that possibly has other\\\\n   ioends linked to it.\\\\n\\\\nDirect I/O\\\\n==========\\\\n\\\\nIn Linux, direct I/O is defined as file I/O that is issued directly to\\\\nstorage, bypassing the pagecache.\\\\nThe ``iomap_dio_rw`` function implements O_DIRECT (direct I/O) reads and\\\\nwrites for files.\\\\n\\\\n.. code-block:: c\\\\n\\\\n ssize_t iomap_dio_rw(struct kiocb *iocb, struct iov_iter *iter,\\\\n                      const struct iomap_ops *ops,\\\\n                      const struct iomap_dio_ops *dops,\\\\n                      unsigned int dio_flags, void *private,\\\\n                      size_t done_before);\\\\n\\\\nThe filesystem can provide the ``dops`` parameter if it needs to perform\\\\nextra work before or after the I/O is issued to storage.\\\\nThe ``done_before`` parameter tells the how much of the request has\\\\nalready been transferred.\\\\nIt is used to continue a request asynchronously when `part of the\\\\nrequest\\\\n<https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=c03098d4b9ad76bca2966a8769dcfe59f7f85103>`_\\\\nhas already been completed synchronously.\\\\n\\\\nThe ``done_before`` parameter should be set if writes for the ``iocb``\\\\nhave been initiated prior to the call.\\\\nThe direction of the I/O is determined from the ``iocb`` passed in.\\\\n\\\\nThe ``dio_flags`` argument can be set to any combination of the\\\\nfollowing values:\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_DIO_FORCE_WAIT``: Wait for the I/O to complete even if the\\\\n   kiocb is not synchronous.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_DIO_OVERWRITE_ONLY``: Perform a pure overwrite for this range\\\\n   or fail with ``-EAGAIN``.\\\\n   This can be used by filesystems with complex unaligned I/O\\\\n   write paths to provide an optimised fast path for unaligned writes.\\\\n   If a pure overwrite can be performed, then serialisation against\\\\n   other I/Os to the same filesystem block(s) is unnecessary as there is\\\\n   no risk of stale data exposure or data loss.\\\\n   If a pure overwrite cannot be performed, then the filesystem can\\\\n   perform the serialisation steps needed to provide exclusive access\\\\n   to the unaligned I/O range so that it can perform allocation and\\\\n   sub-block zeroing safely.\\\\n   Filesystems can use this flag to try to reduce locking contention,\\\\n   but a lot of `detailed checking\\\\n   <https://lore.kernel.org/linux-ext4/20230314130759.642710-1-bfoster@redhat.com/>`_\\\\n   is required to do it `correctly\\\\n   <https://lore.kernel.org/linux-ext4/20230810165559.946222-1-bfoster@redhat.com/>`_.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_DIO_PARTIAL``: If a page fault occurs, return whatever\\\\n   progress has already been made.\\\\n   The caller may deal with the page fault and retry the operation.\\\\n   If the caller decides to retry the operation, it should pass the\\\\n   accumulated return values of all previous calls as the\\\\n   ``done_before`` parameter to the next call.\\\\n\\\\nThese ``struct kiocb`` flags are significant for direct I/O with iomap:\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOCB_NOWAIT``: Turns on ``IOMAP_NOWAIT``.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOCB_SYNC``: Ensure that the device has persisted data to disk\\\\n   before completing the call.\\\\n   In the case of pure overwrites, the I/O may be issued with FUA\\\\n   enabled.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOCB_HIPRI``: Poll for I/O completion instead of waiting for an\\\\n   interrupt.\\\\n   Only meaningful for asynchronous I/O, and only if the entire I/O can\\\\n   be issued as a single ``struct bio``.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOCB_DIO_CALLER_COMP``: Try to run I/O completion from the caller's\\\\n   process context.\\\\n   See ``linux/fs.h`` for more details.\\\\n\\\\nFilesystems should call ``iomap_dio_rw`` from ``->read_iter`` and\\\\n``->write_iter``, and set ``FMODE_CAN_ODIRECT`` in the ``->open``\\\\nfunction for the file.\\\\nThey should not set ``->direct_IO``, which is deprecated.\\\\n\\\\nIf a filesystem wishes to perform its own work before direct I/O\\\\ncompletion, it should call ``__iomap_dio_rw``.\\\\nIf its return value is not an error pointer or a NULL pointer, the\\\\nfilesystem should pass the return value to ``iomap_dio_complete`` after\\\\nfinishing its internal work.\\\\n\\\\nReturn Values\\\\n-------------\\\\n\\\\n``iomap_dio_rw`` can return one of the following:\\\\n\\\\n * A non-negative number of bytes transferred.\\\\n\\\\n * ``-ENOTBLK``: Fall back to buffered I/O.\\\\n   iomap itself will return this value if it cannot invalidate the page\\\\n   cache before issuing the I/O to storage.\\\\n   The ``->iomap_begin`` or ``->iomap_end`` functions may also return\\\\n   this value.\\\\n\\\\n * ``-EIOCBQUEUED``: The asynchronous direct I/O request has been\\\\n   queued and will be completed separately.\\\\n\\\\n * Any of the other negative error codes.\\\\n\\\\nDirect Reads\\\\n------------\\\\n\\\\nA direct I/O read initiates a read I/O from the storage device to the\\\\ncaller's buffer.\\\\nDirty parts of the pagecache are flushed to storage before initiating\\\\nthe read io.\\\\nThe ``flags`` value for ``->iomap_begin`` will be ``IOMAP_DIRECT`` with\\\\nany combination of the following enhancements:\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_NOWAIT``, as defined previously.\\\\n\\\\nCallers commonly hold ``i_rwsem`` in shared mode before calling this\\\\nfunction.\\\\n\\\\nDirect Writes\\\\n-------------\\\\n\\\\nA direct I/O write initiates a write I/O to the storage device from the\\\\ncaller's buffer.\\\\nDirty parts of the pagecache are flushed to storage before initiating\\\\nthe write io.\\\\nThe pagecache is invalidated both before and after the write io.\\\\nThe ``flags`` value for ``->iomap_begin`` will be ``IOMAP_DIRECT |\\\\nIOMAP_WRITE`` with any combination of the following enhancements:\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_NOWAIT``, as defined previously.\\\\n\\\\n * ``IOMAP_OVERWRITE_ONLY``: Allocating blocks and zeroing partial\\\\n   blocks is not allowed.\\\\n   The entire file range must map to a single written or unwritten\\\\n   extent.\\\\n   The file I/O range must be aligned to the filesystem block size\\\\n   if the mapping is unwritten and the filesystem cannot handle zeroing\\\\n   the unaligned regions without exposing stale contents.\\\\n\\\\nCallers commonly hold ``i_rwsem`` in shared or exclusive mode before\\\\ncalling this function.\\\\n\\\\n``struct iomap_dio_ops:``\\\\n-------------------------\\\\n.. code-block:: c\\\\n\\\\n struct iomap_dio_ops {\\\\n     void (*submit_io)(const struct iomap_iter *iter, struct bio *bio,\\\\n                       loff_t file_offset);\\\\n     int (*end_io)(struct kiocb *iocb, ssize_t size, int error,\\\\n                   unsigned flags);\\\\n     struct bio_set *bio_set;\\\\n };\\\\n\\\\nThe fields of this structure are as follows:\\\\n\\\\n  - ``submit_io``: iomap calls this function when it has constructed a\\\\n    ``struct bio`` object for the I/O requested, and wishes to submit it\\\\n    to call\\\\n``iomap_dio_bio_end_io`` to finish the direct I/O.\\\\n\\\\nDAX I/O\\\\n=======\\\\n\\\\nSome storage devices can be directly mapped as memory.\\\\nThese devices support a new access mode Brabete1 Dmitrii Ustiugov2 Yuvraj Patel1 Luo Mai1\\\\n1The University of Edinburgh\\\\n2NTU Singapore\\\\nAbstract\\\\nThis paper presents ServerlessLLM, a locality-enhanced\\\\nserverless inference system for Large Language Models\\\\n(LLMs). ServerlessLLM exploits the substantial capacity and\\\\nbandwidth of storage and memory devices available on GPU\\\\nservers, thereby reducing costly remote checkpoint downloads\\\\nand achieving efficient checkpoint loading. ServerlessLLM\\\\nachieves this through three main contributions: (i) fast LLM\\\\ncheckpoint loading via a novel loading-optimized checkpoint\\\\nformat design, coupled with an efficient multi-tier checkpoint\\\\nloading system; (ii) locality-driven LLM inference with live\\\\nmigration, which allows ServerlessLLM to effectively achieve\\\\nlocality-driven server allocation while preserving the low la-\\\\ntency of ongoing LLM inference; and (iii) locality-aware\\\\nserver allocation, enabling ServerlessLLM to evaluate the sta-\\\\ntus of each server in a cluster and effectively schedule model\\\\nstartup time to capitalize on local checkpoint placement. Our\\\\ncomprehensive experiments, which include microbenchmarks\\\\nand real-world traces, show that ServerlessLLM surpasses\\\\nstate-of-the-art systems by 10 - 200X in latency performance\\\\nwhen running various LLM inference workloads.\\\\n1\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have recently been incor-\\\\nporated into various online applications, including program-\\\\nming assistants [23], search engines [16], and conversational\\\\nbots [51]. These applications process user inputs, like ques-\\\\ntions, by breaking them down into tokens (e.g., words). LLMs\\\\nrespond in an autoregressive fashion, predicting each subse-\\\\nquent token based on the combination of input tokens and\\\\nthose generated so far, until a sentence-ending token (EoS) is\\\\nreached. To streamline this process, LLMs employ key-value\\\\ncaches to store intermediate results, reducing the need for\\\\nrepeated computations.\\\\nServing LLM inference at scale is a challenging problem,\\\\ngiven the substantial GPU resources it requires and the low\\\\nresponse time constraints such interactive services need to\\\\nsatisfy. Furthermore, LLM inference latency is difficult to\\\\npredict because their response time depends on the output\\\\nlength, which can vary significantly [24,39,77], due to iter-\\\\native output token generation. To achieve low latency, pro-\\\\ncessing an LLM request often necessitates the use of several\\\\nGPUs for durations ranging from seconds to minutes. In prac-\\\\ntice, LLM service providers need to host a large number of\\\\nLLMs catered to different developers, leading to significant\\\\nGPU consumption [15] and impeding the sustainability of\\\\nLLM services [19]. As a result, LLM inference services have\\\\nto impose strict caps on the number of requests sent to their\\\\nservices from their users (e.g., 40 messages per 3 hours for\\\\nChatGPT [51]), showing the provider’s current inability to\\\\nsatisfy the LLM inference demand. Researchers [19] project\\\\nthat LLM inference costs may increase by > 50× when it\\\\nreaches the popularity of Google Search.\\\\nTo reduce GPU consumption, LLM service providers are\\\\nexploring serverless inference, as seen in systems like Ama-\\\\nzon SageMaker [60], Azure [46], KServe [11] and Hugging-\\\\nFace [31]. In such setup, developers upload their LLM check-\\\\npoints, including model execution files and model parameter\\\\nfiles, to a storage system. Upon receiving a request, the system\\\\nuses a model loading scheduler to allocate available GPUs for\\\\nstarting up these checkpoints. A request router then directs\\\\nthe inference request to the selected GPUs. Using serverless\\\\nmethod enables providers to efficiently multiplex LLMs on\\\\nshared GPUs, enhancing utilization. Additionally, it offers\\\\ncost benefits to the developers, who pay only per request pro-\\\\ncessed, avoiding the expense of long-term GPU reservations.\\\\nWhile serverless inference holds promise for LLMs, it intro-\\\\nduces significant latency overheads. LLM checkpoints, which\\\\nrange from gigabytes [4,72,86] to terabytes [26] in size due to\\\\ntheir significant number of parameters, incur considerable de-\\\\nlays when downloaded from remote storage. Moreover, these\\\\ncheckpoints consist of numerous tensors, each with varying\\\\nstructures and sizes. The process of loading tensors onto\\\\nGPUs (often involving file deserialisation, memory allocation,\\\\ntensor shape parsing, and more) further contributes to delays.\\\\nWe aim to enhance locality in serverless inference for\\\\n1\\\\narXiv:2401.14351v1  [cs.LG]  25 Jan 2024\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 2 ===\\\\nLLMs. Notably, GPU-based inference servers feature multi-\\\\ntier storage architecture which has substantial host memory\\\\nand storage capabilities, yet these resources are underutilized\\\\nin systems like KServe [11] and Ray Serve [68]. Typically,\\\\nonly part of the host memory is used during model inference,\\\\nand SSDs are minimally employed for caching checkpoints\\\\ndownloaded from the model repository. This underutiliza-\\\\ntion led us to a new system design approach: leveraging the\\\\nmulti-tier storage architecture for local checkpoint storage\\\\nand utilizing their significant storage bandwidth for efficient\\\\ncheckpoint loading.\\\\nHowever, this design approach raises several open concerns:\\\\n(i) Given the complex storage architecture of a GPU server,\\\\nwhich includes multiple GPUs, DRAM, SSDs, and remote\\\\nstorage, all interconnected through various connections like\\\\nPCIe, NVMe and networks, how can we optimize LLM check-\\\\npoint loading to fully leverage the available bandwidth? (ii)\\\\nOpting for servers with pre-loaded checkpoints can improve\\\\nlocality in serverless inference systems, but this might cause\\\\nGPU contention because these servers have ongoing LLM\\\\ninferences with unpredictable completion times. How do we\\\\neffectively handle such GPU contention? (iii) In a distributed\\\\ncluster tasked with loading a model for request processing,\\\\nwhat strategy should be employed to select GPUs to minimize\\\\nthe latency of starting up the model?\\\\nTo address the above, we introduce ServerlessLLM, a\\\\nlocality-enhanced serverless inference system for LLMs. We\\\\nmake several contributions in designing ServerlessLLM:\\\\n(1) Fast LLM checkpoint loading. ServerlessLLM can max-\\\\nimize the storage bandwidth usage of GPU servers for LLM\\\\ncheckpoint loading. It introduces (i) a new loading-optimized\\\\ncheckpoint that supports sequential, chunk-based reading and\\\\nefficient tensor in-memory addressing, and (ii) an efficient\\\\nmulti-tier checkpoint loading system that can harness the sub-\\\\nstantial capacity and bandwidth on a multi-tier memory hier-\\\\narchy, through an in-memory data chunk pool, memory-copy-\\\\nefficient data path, and a multi-stage data loading pipeline.\\\\n(2) Locality-driven LLM inference with live migration. We\\\\nmotivate the need for live migration of LLM inference and\\\\nare the first to implement LLM live migration in serverless\\\\ninference systems to enhance the performance when support-\\\\ning locality-driven inference. The live migration is realized\\\\nusing two new mechanisms: (i) efficient token-based migra-\\\\ntion which determines the smallest necessary set of tokens\\\\nfor accurately moving LLM inference to another server, and\\\\n(ii) two-stage live migration enabling the transfer of LLM\\\\ninference without impacting the user experience in online\\\\napplications.\\\\n(3) Locality-aware server allocation. ServerlessLLM aids\\\\nthe model loading scheduler in serverless inference systems\\\\nby enabling latency-preserving, locality-driven server selec-\\\\ntion. ServerlessLLM’s source code\\\\nis in progress of releasing at https://github.com/Serve\\\\nrlessLLM/ServerlessLLM.\\\\n2\\\\nBackground and Motivation\\\\n2.1\\\\nServerless LLM Inference\\\\nFigure 1 shows the overview of a serverless LLM infer-\\\\nence system. First, an LLM inference request carries a user-\\\\nspecified input prompt, i.e., a list of tokens, based on which an\\\\ninstance of an LLM service iteratively generates tokens, one\\\\ntoken per iteration, based on the prompt and all the previously\\\\ngenerated tokens, until the end-of-sentence token (denoted\\\\nas EoS) is generated, making the total inference time non-\\\\ndeterministic [39,53]. In each iteration, LLM caches interme-\\\\ndiate computations in a KV cache to speed up the next token\\\\ngeneration [39,54].\\\\nLLM inference services are highly compute and memory-\\\\ncapacity intensive, often requiring many GPUs, the number\\\\nof which needs to be adjusted based on demand, to satisfy\\\\nthe compute and memory-capacity requirements. First, LLMs\\\\nhave a large memory footprint featuring billions of parameters\\\\n2\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 3 ===\\\\n[17,21,26,71,72]. Second, LLM inference often powers up\\\\ninteractive services, often characterized by highly dynamic,\\\\nbursty traffic. The necessity to serve LLM inference requests\\\\nunder strict SLOs at a minimal cost makes LLM inference\\\\nservice scaling a challenge for application developers [14,15].\\\\nTo tackle the LLM inference scaling challenge, cloud\\\\nproviders deploy LLMs as a service, i.e., in a serverless man-\\\\nner where the cloud infrastructure can monitor inference re-\\\\nquest traffic to many LLM inference services deployed in a\\\\nshared cluster of GPUs (or custom inference accelerators).\\\\nIn a typical serverless LLM inference system (as shown in\\\\nFigure 1), the controller that receives inference requests and\\\\ndispatches them to GPU-equipped nodes in a shared cluster\\\\nrunning LLM inference service instances, and cloud storage\\\\nthat hosts model checkpoints.\\\\nThe controller features two components, namely request\\\\nrouter and model loading scheduler. The request router steers\\\\nincoming requests to the nodes already running LLM infer-\\\\nence service instances, further referred as warm nodes, or\\\\nasking the model loading scheduler to spin up more instances\\\\nof the LLM service experiencing a load spike. The model\\\\nloading scheduler allocates nodes from the unallocated, cold\\\\nnode pool to start new LLM service instances. The node se-\\\\nlected by the scheduler launches a new inference process in\\\\na container and initializes the runtime environment. The pro-\\\\ncess then downloads the requested model’s checkpoint from\\\\nthe cloud storage and loads it into the GPU memory.\\\\n2.2\\\\nProblems with Serverless LLM Inference\\\\nA serverless inference cluster can multiplex a large number\\\\nof LLMs on shared GPU servers, showing the promise of\\\\nlargely improving resource utilization and reducing the cost\\\\nof deploying LLMs. This approach benefits from the dynamic\\\\nallocation of resources, allowing for more efficient use of\\\\nGPU servers and potentially lowering user expenses.\\\\nWhile promising, deploying LLMs onto serverless infer-\\\\nence systems often incurs substantial latency overheads. We\\\\nobserved several primary reasons:\\\\n(1) Costly checkpoint download from model repositories.\\\\nServerless functions are designed to separate computation\\\\nand data. AWS, for example, recommends downloading large\\\\ndata from S3 [5,6]. For instance, downloading an LLM check-\\\\npoint with size 130GB (e.g., LLaMA-2-70B [72]) from S3 or\\\\nblob storage takes at least 26 seconds with a fast commodity\\\\nnetwork (5GB/s [14]).\\\\n(2) Costly checkpoint loading from storage devices. Even\\\\nmodel checkpoints can be stored locally in NVMe SSDs,\\\\nloading checkpoints into GPU still takes more than tens of\\\\nseconds (detailed in §7.2). For example, loading OPT-30B\\\\ninto 4 GPUs takes 34 seconds using PyTorch, and LLaMA-\\\\n2-70b into 8 GPUs takes 84 seconds. On the other hand, the\\\\ninference latency per token is around 100ms [41], which is\\\\nsignificantly smaller than the loading latency. Additionally,\\\\nthe startup latency of a serving instance (often a container or\\\\nprocess) often takes several seconds [41], with the potential\\\\nto be further reduced to below a second [42,64,76]. Hence, a\\\\nsignificant component of LLM startup latency is attributed to\\\\nthe loading of a checkpoint.\\\\n2.3\\\\nCurrent Solutions\\\\nTo improve the latency performance when supporting LLMs,\\\\nexisting solutions show a variety of issues:\\\\n(1) Over-subscribing model instances. The existing solu-\\\\ntions [7,79], designed to avoid model download and loading in\\\\na serverless inference cluster, often involve over-subscribing\\\\nGPUs, creating an excessive number of model replicas for\\\\npeak demand. For example, AWS Serverless Inference [7]\\\\ncan keep a certain number of warm instances to mitigate the\\\\neffects of slow cold starts. While this approach is feasible\\\\nfor conventional small models (e.g., ResNet [30]), it becomes\\\\nproblematic for LLMs due to their significantly higher de-\\\\nmand on expensive GPUs.\\\\n(2) Caching models in host memory. Additionally, there are\\\\nsolutions [29,36,83] that maintain model checkpoint caches\\\\nin the host memory of GPU servers, thereby avoiding model\\\\ndownloads. While being effective for conventional small mod-\\\\nels (e.g., up to a couple of GBs [36]) or LoRA adapters [62],\\\\nrelying on a host-memory-based cache only is not sufficient\\\\nfor LLMs. With LLMs, cache misses are common in these\\\\nsystems, resulting in excessive model downloads, and com-\\\\npromising model startup latency (with more details presented\\\\nin §7.4).\\\\n(3) Deploying additional storage servers. There are solu-\\\\ntions [14] advocating for the deployment of additional storage\\\\nservers to cache model checkpoints in a local cluster. How-\\\\never, recent trace studies [14] have revealed that download-\\\\ning a model can take over 20 seconds through an optimized\\\\npipeline connected to local commodity storage servers, even\\\\nif it is equipped with a 100 Gbps NIC. While the further\\\\nadoption of high-speed networks (e.g., 200 Gbps Ethernet or\\\\nInfiniBand) can reduce this latency, the cost of deploying the\\\\nadditional storage servers and high-bandwidth networks often\\\\nincurs formidable expenses [13,28].\\\\n3\\\\nLocality-Enhanced Serverless Inference\\\\nWe now introduce ServerlessLLM – a novel low-latency\\\\nserverless inference system designed for LLMs. Serverless-\\\\nLLM addresses the two issues we highlighted in the previous\\\\nsection – very high model download time and inefficient load-\\\\ning the model into the GPU memory from the local storage.\\\\nOur design is motivated by a simple observation that GPU-\\\\nbased servers used for inference incorporate a multi-tier stor-\\\\nage hierarchy having substantial capacity and bandwidth.\\\\n3\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 4 ===\\\\nFrom a capacity perspective, GPU servers are integrated with\\\\nsubstantial memory capabilities, hosting terabyte-scale mem-\\\\nory, tens of terabytes in NVMe SSDs, and up to hundreds of\\\\nterabytes in SATA SSDs [49]. From a bandwidth perspective,\\\\nGPU servers often comprise several GPUs, each connected to\\\\nthe host memory via a dedicated PCIe link. Similarly, NVMe\\\\nSSDs also connect via their own PCIe channels. For instance,\\\\nan 8-GPU server with PCIe 4.0 offers 256GB/s bandwidth be-\\\\ntween host memory and GPU, and 10-30 GB/s between host\\\\nmemory and NVMe SSD (in RAID 0). The Grace-Hopper\\\\narchitecture improves CPU-GPU bandwidth to 900GB/s [48].\\\\nAdditionally, we observe that in serverless inference context, a\\\\nsignificant portion of the GPU servers’ host memory and stor-\\\\nage devices are under-utilized, leaving a significant portion\\\\nof the bandwidth and capacity unused.\\\\nBased on the above observation, we want to explore\\\\nlocality-enhanced serverless inference for LLMs where the\\\\nsystem exploits the unused capacity and bandwidth to store\\\\nthe models locally and load the models faster, thereby reduc-\\\\ning the latency. In realizing our design, we anticipate three\\\\nimportant concerns that our design should consider.\\\\n(1) Multi-tiered storage hierarchy support. Existing check-\\\\npoint and model loaders such as PyTorch [56], Tensor-\\\\nFlow [70], and ONNX Runtime [59] primarily focus on fa-\\\\ncilitating the training and debugging of models. However,\\\\nthese tools are not optimized for reading performance, which\\\\nbecomes a significant issue in a serverless inference environ-\\\\nment. In such environments, model checkpoints are stored\\\\nonce but need to be loaded and accessed repeatedly across\\\\nmultiple GPUs. This lack of optimization for read opera-\\\\ntions leads to substantial loading delays, impacting overall\\\\nefficiency. Solutions such as Safetensors [32] can improve\\\\nloading performance. However, as we show in Section 7,\\\\nthey still do not exploit the full potential of the multi-tiered\\\\nmemory hierarchy. ServerlessLLM design needs to consider\\\\nperformance as a key aspect such that it can harness the entire\\\\nmemory hierarchy’s capacity and bandwidth efficiently. To ad-\\\\ndress the concern, we discuss the design of loading optimized\\\\ncheckpoints and the model manager in Section 4.\\\\n(2) Strong locality-driven inference. Designing an efficient\\\\nmodel loader is not enough; one needs to have a central entity\\\\nthat can recognize the checkpoint placements and the current\\\\nload on each GPU server to enhance locality-driven inference.\\\\nExisting serverless systems randomly assign models to avail-\\\\nable GPUs overlooking the locality factor. Despite cluster\\\\nscheduling systems such as Sparrow [52] focusing on locality\\\\noptimization, they cause significant queueing delays if the\\\\nassigned GPU is busy. Distributed model serving systems\\\\n(such as ClockWork [29] and Shepherd [85]) can consider\\\\nlocality. They however either rely on the accurate prediction\\\\nof model inference time, making them struggle with LLMs, or\\\\nthey preempt ongoing model inferences, leading to significant\\\\ndowntime and redundant computations. Hence, Serverless-\\\\nLLM needs to accommodate a new approach that prioritizes\\\\ncheckpoint locality while avoiding interrupting ongoing LLM\\\\ninference. We discuss the design of such an approach in Sec-\\\\ntion 5.\\\\n(3) Resource allocation optimized for locality. Serverless-\\\\nLLM is designed to minimize the model startup latency by\\\\nleveraging the local checkpoint placement. The model load-\\\\ning scheduler plays a crucial role in allocating GPU resources\\\\nto achieve that goal. However, the scheduler needs to allocate\\\\nresources after careful consideration of the entire cluster sta-\\\\ntus. Many factors may influence the overall startup latency,\\\\nsuch as the difference in the bandwidth offered by each layer\\\\nin the memory hierarchy. There may be instances where it is\\\\nbeneficial to move the current inference execution to a new\\\\nGPU than to allocate the request to a GPU where the model\\\\nmay have to be loaded from the storage media. Hence, Server-\\\\nlessLLM needs to accurately estimate the startup times con-\\\\nsidering the cluster status and accordingly allocate resources\\\\nto minimize startup time. We discuss the design of such a\\\\nstartup-time-optimized allocation approach in Section 6.\\\\nSummary. ServerlessLLM ensures that the model loading\\\\ntime is minimal to improve the overall latency by harnessing\\\\nthe memory and storage capacity and bandwidth available on\\\\nthe local GPU. The model manager we describe next handles\\\\nefficient loading of the checkpoints. ServerlessLLM relies on\\\\nthe modified scheduler to ensure that the inference requests\\\\nare assigned to those GPUs that already have the model data\\\\nstored locally to avoid downloading.\\\\n4\\\\nFast LLM Checkpoint Loading\\\\nWe create loading-optimized checkpoints for efficient loading\\\\nwith a model manager and further enhance performance with\\\\nan efficient multi-tier checkpoint storage system.\\\\n4.1\\\\nLoading-Optimized Checkpoints\\\\nWe operate under a set of assumptions about the checkpoints.\\\\nThe checkpoints have: (i) Model execution files which de-\\\\nfine the model architecture. Depending on the framework, the\\\\nformat varies; TensorFlow typically uses protobuf files [69],\\\\nwhile PyTorch employs Python scripts [55]. Beyond architec-\\\\nture, these files detail the size and shape of each tensor and\\\\ninclude a model parallelism plan. This plan specifies the target\\\\nGPU for each tensor during checkpoint loading. (ii) Model\\\\nparameter files which stores the binary data of parameters in\\\\nan LLM. Tensors within these files can be arranged in any\\\\nsequence. Runtimes such as PyTorch may also store tensor\\\\nshapes as indices to calculate the offset and size for each\\\\ntensor.\\\\nServerlessLLM converts the given checkpoint into a new\\\\nloading-optimized format. The conversion has two primary\\\\ngoals: (i) Support sequential chunk-based reading: To ensure\\\\n4\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 5 ===\\\\nGPU\\\\nInference Process\\\\nModel Manager\\\\nModel execution files\\\\nGPU\\\\n(model name, GPU ids)\\\\nSynchronisation\\\\n2\\\\n1\\\\nModel\\\\nInitialization \\\\nFunction\\\\nBinary Data\\\\nTensor index file\\\\nTensor data files\\\\nBase address\\\\nGPU 0\\\\nBase address\\\\nGPU 1\\\\nLoading-optimised checkpoint\\\\n<GPU id, base address>\\\\nModel\\\\nDefinition\\\\nLoading\\\\nFunction\\\\n<tensor.name, GPU id, offset, size>\\\\nModel Object\\\\nInitialized\\\\nModel Object\\\\nIssue loading to GPU\\\\nFigure 2: Checkpoint loading process.\\\\nefficient sequential reading, tensors for each GPU are grouped\\\\nin separate files. These files contain only the binary data of\\\\nmodel parameters and exclude metadata such as tensor shapes,\\\\nfacilitating large chunk reading. (ii) Support efficient tensor\\\\naddressing: We create an index file that maps tensor names\\\\nto a tuple of GPU id, offset, and size, facilitating the efficient\\\\nrestoration of tensors. The tensors are aligned with memory\\\\nword sizes, facilitating direct computation of memory address\\\\nand avoiding deserialization.\\\\nServerlessLLM has an in-server model manager to load\\\\nthe loading-optimized checkpoints. The loading process is\\\\nillustrated in Figure 2. ServerlessLLM model manager al-\\\\nlocates memory on GPUs and preloads the binary data of\\\\nthe checkpoints (see 1 ). The preloading operation can ben-\\\\nefit from the sequential chunk-based read design. While the\\\\nmodel is needed, the inference process can efficiently obtain\\\\nthe memory address of the checkpoints in the GPU (see 2 ).\\\\nSpecifically, ServerlessLLM provides a loading function for\\\\nLLM libraries. This function acquires the base addresses for\\\\neach GPU (i.e., CUDA IPC handles). By querying the tensor\\\\nindex file, this function iterates through the model and set\\\\neach tensor’s memory address (i.e., base + offset). To ensure\\\\nthe model is fully initialized before inference, the inference\\\\nprocess and the model manager perform a synchronization.\\\\n4.2\\\\nEfficient Multi-Tier Checkpoint Loading\\\\nTo boost the checkpoint loading, we design an efficient\\\\nmulti-tier checkpoint loading subsystem, integrated within\\\\nthe model manager. This subsystem incorporates several tech-\\\\nniques:\\\\nIn-memory data chunk pool. We’ve developed an in-\\\\nmemory data chunk pool in ServerlessLLM with three main\\\\ngoals: (i) Utilizing parallel PCIe links. To mitigate the bottle-\\\\nneck caused by a single PCIe link from storage when loading\\\\nmultiple models into GPUs, we employ parallel DRAM-to-\\\\nGPU PCIe links to facilitate concurrent checkpoint loading\\\\nacross GPUs. (ii) Supporting application-specific controls.\\\\nOur memory pool surpasses simple caching by providing\\\\nAPIs for the allocation and deallocation of memory. This\\\\nenables fine-grained management of cached or evicted data\\\\nchunks, based on specific requirements of the application.\\\\n(iii) Mitigating memory fragmentation. We address latency\\\\nand space inefficiencies caused by memory fragmentation by\\\\nusing fixed-size memory chunks for allocation and dealloca-\\\\ntion.\\\\nEfficient data path. We’ve created an efficient data path in\\\\nour model manager with two main strategies: (i) Exploiting\\\\ndirect file access. We use direct file access (e.g., ‘O_DIRECT’\\\\nin Linux) to avoid excessive data copying by directly read-\\\\ning data into user space. This method outperforms memory-\\\\nmapped files (mmap), currently adopted in high-speed loaders\\\\nsuch as Safetensors [32], which rely on system cache and lack\\\\nconsistent performance guarantees (critical for low latency\\\\nscenarios). (ii) Exploiting pinned memory. We utilize pinned\\\\nmemory to eliminate redundant data copying between DRAM\\\\nand GPU. This approach allows direct copying to the GPU\\\\nwith minimal CPU involvement, ensuring efficient use of PCIe\\\\nbandwidth with a single thread.\\\\nMulti-stage data loading pipeline. We accommodate a multi-\\\\nstage data loading pipeline to maximize throughput: (i) Sup-\\\\nport for multiple storage interfaces. ServerlessLLM offers\\\\ndedicated function calls for various storage interfaces, includ-\\\\ning local storage (e.g., NVMe, SATA), remote storage (e.g.,\\\\nS3 object store [5]), and in-memory storage (pinned mem-\\\\nory). It utilizes appropriate methods for efficient data access\\\\nin each case. (ii) Optimization for intra-stage throughput. To\\\\nleverage modern storage devices’ high concurrency, Server-\\\\nlessLLM employs multiple threads for reading data within\\\\neach storage tier, improving bandwidth utilization. (iii) Ef-\\\\nficient inter-stage coordination. ServerlessLLM uses a task\\\\nqueue-based pipeline for extensibility and low latency. Load-\\\\ning threads read storage chunks and enqueue their indices\\\\n(offset and size) for the loading threads in the next tier.\\\\n5\\\\nLocality-Driven LLM Inference\\\\nwith Live Migration\\\\nIn this section, we describe how ServerlessLLM achieves\\\\nlive migration for LLM inference, which enables locality-\\\\ndriven model startup while avoiding affecting ongoing LLM\\\\ninference.\\\\n5.1\\\\nNeed for Live Migration\\\\nWe consider a simple example to analyze the performance\\\\nof different current approaches in supporting the checkpoint\\\\nlocality.
